plan.question: Can an activation probe on an open-weights experiment agent's own activations catch fabricated, tampered or misreported results as well as an LLM transcript monitor does?
plan.hypothesis: A difference-of-means probe matches or beats an LLM transcript monitor at 5% false positives, and adds 10+ points combined [Bergen et al.]

compute_axis.quantity: Sampled rollouts per task and trap condition in the ExpTrap test set (24 tasks x 6 conditions)

held_fixed: Agent: Qwen 3.8 27B BF16, default thinking effort, mini-SWE-agent scaffold
Probe aggregation fixed in advance: max over tokens in a passage, then max over passages
ExpTrap used only for testing; no layer, probe weight or monitor prompt tuned on it
Primary metric: recall at 5% false-positive rate, honest runs within the same condition
Monitor prompt gets same tuning effort as probe: three variants chosen on Arm R

predictions.if_lever: A probe on the agent's activations matches or beats the LLM monitor on planted-trap tests, and adds 10+ recall points to it.
predictions.if_not: The probe is no better than a bag-of-words or token-embedding control, or the 2x2 reader test shows no extra gain from the agent's own activations; the signal is in the text.
predictions.decision_rule: P1 recall at 5% FPR on ExpTrap >= B1 recall, and B1+P minus B1 >= 10 points means I6 holds; P1 no better than B5 or B6 means it is a text classifier; 2x2 interaction about zero means the signal is in the text.
predictions.noise_rule: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals resampled by task; the budget can detect differences of roughly 15 to 20 points, not 3 to 8.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it flags the 27B agent may rarely cheat and that power is limited to 15 to 20 point gaps.

plan.compute_tested_why: The test compares probe against monitor methods on fixed rollouts; it does not vary a quantity that more parallel compute buys.
plan.scored_against: Ground-truth labels from sandbox instrumentation (file hashes, mirror log, test-label read log, run registry compared with report) and construction (passing an impossible split = cheating), with judge plus human audit for disclosure and spin in C1 and C5.

[QUESTION, PLAN question] Can a probe on an open-weights experiment agent's own activations catch fabricated, tampered or misreported results?
[QUESTION, PLAN baseline] The comparison is against a language-model monitor reading the transcript.
[HYPOTHESIS, PLAN hypothesis] A difference-of-means probe should match or beat that monitor at 5% false positives.
[HYPOTHESIS, PLAN hypothesis] Combining probe and monitor should add 10 or more points.

[TEST, GIVEN budget] The whole study runs on rented GPUs within a $1,000 budget.
[TEST, PLAN phases] A pilot must first show a shortcut rate of at least 0.1.
[IF_LEVER, PLAN predictions.if_lever] The probe matches or beats the monitor on planted traps and adds 10 or more recall points.
[IF_NOT, PLAN predictions.if_not] The probe is no better than text-only controls, so the signal is in the text.

[LIMITS, PLAN noise_rule] Only gaps of roughly 15 to 20 points are detectable, not 3 to 8.
[LIMITS, PLAN compute_tested_why] The test varies nothing extra parallel compute buys, so it says nothing about GPU scaling.

pick.title: Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation

plan.option_title: Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation
plan.question: Does a validated GPU spectral turbulence simulation on one rented 8-GPU node show cost per large-eddy turnover rising with Reynolds number, as the claimed Re³ law predicts?
plan.hypothesis: Cost per large-eddy turnover will scale roughly as N⁴, i.e. Rλ⁶, so 100× compute buys only about 2.15× in Rλ [wiki_dns].

compute_axis.quantity: grid points per side N at fixed small-scale resolution (k_max η ≈ 1.35), which sets Rλ and cost

held_fixed: k_max η ≈ 1.35
Courant number ≈ 0.022
same pseudo-spectral scheme (integrating factor, AB2, phase-shift de-aliasing, forcing |k|≤2)
same JHTDB starting field low-pass filtered
5 T_L of statistics per rung

predictions.if_lever: Fitted exponents near a≈2/3 (Rλ∝N^a), b≈4 (dollars per T_L∝N^b), c≈6 (∝Rλ^c): extra compute buys little Reynolds number.
predictions.if_not: Fitted exponents differ clearly from 2/3, 4 and 6 with confidence intervals excluding them, e.g. because u′ and ε do not stay fixed across rungs.
predictions.decision_rule: Compare fitted a, b, c with 2/3, 4, 6 using confidence intervals; the Re³ scaling is supported if the intervals contain the predictions.
predictions.noise_rule: Report confidence intervals on the exponent fits; JHTDB's own scatter (Rλ std 10.8, window means 406.6–432.9) sets the statistical tolerances; fits made with and without the latency-dominated 128³ rung.
predictions.expected_why: The file's own derivation from JHTDB definitions gives N⁴ ∝ Rλ⁶ and the plan expects a≈2/3, b≈4, c≈6.

plan.compute_tested_why: The resolution ladder 128³ to 1024³ varies N, which is what more parallel GPU compute buys, and measures dollars and Rλ at each rung.
plan.scored_against: JHTDB isotropic1024 published time-averaged statistics (Rλ 418, ε 0.103, E 0.705, spectrum), stored frames, and the predicted exponents a≈2/3, b≈4, c≈6.

C4: report u′, L, T_L, ε/(u′³/L) on every rung to test the fixed u′ and ε assumption

restructuring.sequential_part: Time stepping: about 50,280 sequential steps at 1024³, each depending on the previous one.
restructuring.method: Each 3D FFT is split across 8 GPUs in slabs, with an NCCL all-to-all transpose, so the transforms within one time step run in parallel.
restructuring.baseline_sequential: One-GPU runs on A6000 and H100 for the 128³ and 256³ rungs and for C1 tests.
restructuring.condition: The FFT must not be dominated by communication; P2 measures seconds per step and the FFT/all-to-all breakdown on A100, H100, B200 before the main spend.

scope_gap: Cannot reach new physics or a Reynolds-number record; record is 32,768³ at Rλ≈2,550
Memory and cost ceiling at about 2048³ (Rλ≈664) on one B200 node
Ladder only spans Rλ about 104 to 418 at fixed k_max η
Does not cover the Re = 1600 Taylor–Green reference data

novelty.closest_prior: JHTDB isotropic1024 is a published 1024³ pseudo-spectral DNS at Rλ 418 with stored fields; Wikipedia states DNS operations grow as Re³. Neither gives measured dollars per turnover on rented GPUs.
novelty.left_open: A measured dollars-versus-Rλ curve on rented hardware, with fitted exponents and an open validated solver, is not given by the cited sources.

limits: Cost per step is only bandwidth arithmetic until the bake-off measures it. Only one node and one forcing scheme; JHTDB scheme details may leave a mismatch floor. JHTDB cutout access was unconfirmed (HTTP 503).
plan.test_summary: Build a GPU spectral turbulence solver, check it against the public JHTDB 1024³ run (Rλ 418), then run a 128³ to 1024³ ladder on rented H100 nodes to measure how dollars per turnover grow with Rλ, comparing with the Re³ law [wiki_dns].

records.card: **W3 · Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation.** R2 · physical · top pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Does a validated GPU spectral turbulence simulation on one rented 8-GPU node show cost per large-eddy turnover rising with Reynolds number, as the claimed Re³ law predicts? **What is known.** JHTDB isotropic1024 is a published 1024³ pseudo-spectral DNS at Rλ 418 with stored fields; Wikipedia states DNS operations grow as Re³. Neither gives measured dollars per turnover on rented GPUs. A measured dollars-versus-Rλ curve on rented hardware, with fitted exponents and an open validated solver, is not given by the cited sources. **Hypothesis.** Cost per large-eddy turnover will scale roughly as N⁴, i.e. Rλ⁶, so 100× compute buys only about 2.15× in Rλ [wiki_dns]. **Restructuring.** Time stepping: about 50,280 sequential steps at 1024³, each depending on the previous one. Each 3D FFT is split across 8 GPUs in slabs, with an NCCL all-to-all transpose, so the transforms within one time step run in parallel. **If compute is the lever.** Fitted exponents near a≈2/3 (Rλ∝N^a), b≈4 (dollars per T_L∝N^b), c≈6 (∝Rλ^c): extra compute buys little Reynolds number. **If not.** Fitted exponents differ clearly from 2/3, 4 and 6 with confidence intervals excluding them, e.g. because u′ and ε do not stay fixed across rungs. **Test.** Build a GPU spectral turbulence solver, check it against the public JHTDB 1024³ run (Rλ 418), then run a 128³ to 1024³ ladder on rented H100 nodes to measure how dollars per turnover grow with Rλ, comparing with the Re³ law [wiki_dns]. *Compute axis.* Grid points per side N at fixed small-scale resolution (k_max η ≈ 1.35), which sets Rλ and cost: 128–1,024 grid points per side, 4 levels. Closest prior: 1,024 [jhtdb_readme], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search. **Check first.** Reproduce JHTDB isotropic1024 time-averaged Rλ of 418 with our 1024³ solver [jhtdb_readme] Tolerance: 418 ± 15 (also ε 0.103 ± 10%, E 0.705 ± 3%, E(k) ratio 0.9–1.1 for 3≤k≤100). **Would not show.** Cost per step is only bandwidth arithmetic until the bake-off measures it. Only one node and one forcing scheme; JHTDB scheme details may leave a mismatch floor. JHTDB cutout access was unconfirmed (HTTP 503). *Cost.* Plans $319.70 of the $1,000 budget over 51.3 machine-hours, leaving $680.30. Full scale: Reaching Rλ≈2,550 at JHTDB's k_max η would cost about (2550/418)⁶ ≈ 51,500× the 1024³ cost per T_L, roughly $0.9M–2.7M per T_L, $900,000, 900× the budget. 11 cost flags in the block. **Halted at cost record broken.** gate_ref at phases.P4.gate.on: "c2_pass" is not a number id; [QUESTION, PLAN question] Does a validated GPU spectral turbulence simulation on one rented eight-GPU node show cost rising with Reynolds number as claimed?
[QUESTION, GIVEN budget] The whole study must fit within the $1,000 budget.
[HYPOTHESIS, SOURCE wiki_dns] Direct simulation of turbulence needs operations that grow as Reynolds number cubed.
[HYPOTHESIS, PLAN hypothesis] Cost per large-eddy turnover should scale roughly as grid points per side to the fourth power.
[HYPOTHESIS, PLAN hypothesis] So a hundredfold more compute buys only a small gain in Reynolds number.
[TEST, PLAN compute_axis] The ladder runs 128, 256, 512 and 1024 grid points per side, a span of 8.
[TEST, PLAN arms] A 1024 cubed run reproduces the public JHTDB turbulence baseline at Reynolds number 418.
[TEST, PLAN held_fixed] Small-scale resolution, time-step size, numerical scheme and starting field stay fixed across rungs.
[TEST, PLAN phases] One gate requires all solver correctness checks to pass, indicator 1, before renting the multi-GPU node.
[TEST, PLAN phases] Another gate requires step time at 1024 cubed of at most 0.6 seconds.
[TEST, PLAN numbers] Planned spend is $319.70 over 51.3 machine-hours, leaving $680.30 unallocated.
[IF_LEVER, PLAN predictions.if_lever] Fitted exponents near two thirds, four and six would show extra compute buys little Reynolds number.
[IF_NOT, PLAN predictions.if_not] Exponents clearly differing, with confidence intervals excluding those values, would contradict the claimed scaling.
[LIMITS, PLAN limits] Cost per step is only bandwidth arithmetic until the bake-off measures it.
[LIMITS, PLAN limits] Only one node and one forcing scheme are used.
[LIMITS, PLAN scope_gap] Reaching Reynolds number 2,550 would cost about $900,000 per turnover, or 900 times the budget.

plan.hypothesis: At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844].

held_fixed: Model SmolVLA 0.45B with LeRobot defaults (lr 1e-4, AdamW betas 0.9/0.95, 1000 warmup, cosine to 2.5e-6, chunk 50)
Batch size 64
Dataset lerobot/libero with pinned revision and pinned LeRobot commit
Nested task-stratified data subsets from one fixed shuffle seed
Evaluation: 50 episodes per task x 40 tasks, same seed, init_states true, n_action_steps chosen once before scoring the grid
Per-run cosine schedule with scheduler_decay_steps equal to steps in arm B

predictions.if_lever: At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success.
predictions.if_not: At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points.
predictions.decision_rule: P1: if the 15k to 50k change in average success is under 3 points at every data level, data-bound (not compute-bound); if 3 points or more, compute still pays. P2: 100% vs 25% data at 50k steps gap of at least 10 points means data is binding.
predictions.noise_rule: Count an effect as real only if it exceeds both the paired evaluation interval (about +/-2.1 points between two 2,000-episode cells; McNemar and task bootstrap) and twice the training-seed standard deviation from the B' replicates plus arm A.
predictions.expected_why: The paper says the model can be trained for far fewer steps without significant loss, and data scarcity (about 11 demos per task at 25%) should bind.

plan.compute_tested_why: Training steps vary 10x (5k to 50k) and trainable parameters about 4.5x, independently of data fraction, though far below the 100-1000x frontier range.
plan.scored_against: Simulated LIBERO success flag over 2,000 rollouts per checkpoint (50 per task x 40 tasks), compared within the grid against the B (100% data, 50k steps) cell and its B' replicate, and the harness against the published pi0.5 score.

arms.what: Evaluation-only harness check: score lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned with n_action_steps=10
Replication gate: 2 seeds (1000, 1001), LeRobot LIBERO command unchanged, 100% data, default schedule, 100k steps
Compute x data grid: 12 runs, data in {10,25,50,100}% x steps in {5k,15k,50k}, decay steps = steps
4 seed replicates (seed 1001) of B's four 50k-step cells
Trainable capacity: train_expert_only=false freeze_vision_encoder=false, data 25% and 100%, 50k steps
Missing-channel analogue: wrist camera image2 removed, 100% data, 5k/15k/50k steps
Start from lerobot/smolvla_base (pretrained on another robot), data 25% and 100%, 50k steps

baseline.what: SmolVLA 0.45B published LIBERO average success (90/96/92/71 on Spatial/Object/Goal/Long), 100k steps at batch 64, no robot pretraining

anchor.what: Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 400 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%.
anchor.tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3

checks: Harness gate: pi0.5 checkpoint >= 94% on 400 episodes before any training
Replication gate: arm A mean within +/-5 of 87.3; early soft gate: 20k checkpoint at about hour 6 below 70% pauses the grid
Score arm A at n_action_steps 10 and 50, pick one before scoring grid
Subset lists saved and nested (10 in 25 in 50 in 100) with per-task counts
Data monotonicity at equal steps within noise
Training loss falls progressively across 5k/15k/50k at fixed data
Compute ledger x-axis in GPU-hours from logs, not nominal steps
Arm D saved policy config takes one image input
Save per-episode outcomes (task, init-state index, success)
Paired evaluation: same seed and init states, McNemar plus bootstrap over 40 tasks

phases.what: Install pinned LeRobot; harness gate (A0); throughput and memory test at batch 64 for expert-only and full fine-tuning on 40 GB; measure evaluation speed; check arm D input change and arm E key names

gate.else: Fix simulator, rendering or library versions before training anything

phases.stop_rule: If measured throughput is under 3,500 steps per A100-hour, cut arm E, then shrink B' to two cells, then run arm C at 100% data only; if evaluation cannot keep pace, drop to 20 episodes per task

phases.what: GPUs 0-1: arm A (100k steps). GPUs 2-3: arm C. GPUs 4-7: arm B 50k cells, then B'. Score arm A 20k checkpoint at about hour 6.

gate.else: Pause the grid and debug

phases.what: GPUs 0-1: arm E. GPU 2: arm D 50k. GPUs 3-4: B 15k x4, B 5k x4, D 15k and D 5k. GPUs 5-7: score wave-1 checkpoints.
Remaining evaluations; copy results off the instance; fit logit(success) on grid B for the compute-data exchange rate

plan.question: Can an equation distilled from a sparse neural residual, trained on real cloth motion capture, beat the best hand-designed aerodynamic fix on unseen speeds?
plan.hypothesis: Law from a sparse residual network can cut cloth error on fast unseen motions by at least 15% versus best hand-designed drag.

compute_axis.quantity: Fraction of the real-data volume used in the planted-law positive control (data size, not compute; the file says the experiment is not compute-bound)

held_fixed: Same 500-evaluation CMA-ES budget for every model (B1, B2, candidate)
Splits made strictly by recording, never by window
Same real recorded corner trajectories drive the simulator
Mass from published areal densities
Pre-registered thresholds (15% on speed split, 2% on negative control)

predictions.if_lever: Distilled law has at least 15% lower median error than best hand-designed drag on 32 fast recordings, interval excluding zero, no worse than black-box.
predictions.if_not: Distilled law roughly equals the hand-designed baseline (rediscovering textbook drag), or black-box residual fails to beat it; more or denser data needed, not compute.
predictions.decision_rule: Primary claim holds if candidate median error is >=15% lower than B2 on the speed split over 32 test recordings, paired-bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0, and candidate is no worse than B3; same functional form selected in >=4 of 5 seeds.
predictions.noise_rule: Paired bootstrap 95% CI over test recordings; 5 seeds per primary split; form stability in >=4 of 5 seeds; negative controls (no planted term, time-shuffled targets) must improve held-out error by less than 2%.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it lists four outcomes and notes the work is limited by data and validation, not FLOPs.

plan.compute_tested_why: The file says the experiment is limited by data and validation, not FLOPs (NOT COMPUTE-BOUND). The only varied quantity is data volume in the synthetic control, which parallel compute does not buy.
plan.scored_against: Held-out recorded marker positions, scored by the dataset paper's mass-weighted mean marker distance (eq. 1) on held-out speed, motion, size and fabric splits, compared with baseline B2 (best hand-designed aerodynamic term, same tuning budget).

checks: Loader unit test: error of a recording against itself is 0; rigid non-moving sheet gives a sanity upper bound
Positive control: planted quadratic normal drag and an angle-of-attack drag term recovered (sympy-equivalent, coefficients within 20%) in >=4 of 5 seeds at 100% data, with 0.1 mm and 1 mm noise
Mismatched-internals control with different mesh resolution and bending stiffness
Negative control: no planted term, and real data with residual targets shuffled in time; improvement under 2%
Speed scaling: term roughly proportional to v^2; predicted about 8x larger on fast recordings (5-11x)
Density scaling: per-mass effect about 1/areal density, about 2.9x larger on polyester
Dissipation: f.v <= 0 over observed range and invariant to normal sign flip
Baseline sanity: B2 in-sample error within about 1.5x of published under 1 cm
Hanger to hands in-distribution control
Optional external replication on Blanco-Mulero fling data with frozen form

fields.anchor.what: Best hand-designed-drag baseline's in-sample error on DIN A2 table cases should be within about 1.5x of the Coltraro model's published under 1 cm [coltraro_pdf].

pick.title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis for long-tail skills

plan.option_title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis (model sizing for the long tail)
plan.question: Do small robot policies drop rare skills because of too few samples, no spare capacity, overwriting by common tasks, or narrow memorized storage?
plan.hypothesis: Rare-task success of small behaviour-cloning policies improves with width beyond a task-difficulty baseline, as in the OLMo result [huang], because common-task updates interfere with rare skills.

compute_axis.quantity: Policy hidden width (MLP width in Meta-World stage; parameters from about 5K to about 9M)

held_fixed: 100K Adam steps at batch 1,024 for every width (Meta-World)
Same task identities, with task-to-rank order re-drawn per seed
50 fresh-position evaluation episodes per task
Same expert demonstrations (5,000 successful episodes per task)
3 seeds per cell

predictions.if_lever: Gap between common-task and rare-task success shrinks as width grows when tasks are unevenly sampled, beyond the uniform-sampling baseline, and matched single-task models succeed.
predictions.if_not: The width-by-frequency interaction is near zero (under 5 points per width doubling), so long-tail failure is just too few rare-task samples.
predictions.decision_rule: H1 refuted if the interaction CI includes 0 and its point estimate is under 5 points per width doubling.
predictions.noise_rule: Logistic mixed model success ~ log2(width) x log(pi) + (1|task) + (1|seed), hierarchical bootstrap over seeds then tasks, 3 seeds, tasks pooled into frequency quintiles, hypotheses pre-registered.
predictions.expected_why: The file gives no expected outcome; the plan is built so that each of H1 to H5 can fail, and prior evidence is only OLMo and LLM.

plan.compute_tested_why: Width (parameter count) is swept over 7 values with step count held fixed, with a 5x longer training control at small widths.
plan.scored_against: Per-task rollout success in simulation (Meta-World fresh positions, LIBERO-90 rollouts) with Wilson intervals, compared with uniform sampling (beta = 0), single-task matched models, tuned plain-sum training and random-direction edits.

arms.what: Width x task-frequency sweep on Meta-World MT50, beta in {0,1,1.5}, 7 widths, 3 seeds (63 runs)
Widths 32, 64, 128 at beta=1 with 5x steps (9 runs)
Single-task models on each of the 5 rarest tasks with same sample count (45 runs)
Group gradient projection, temperature upsampling T=2, tuned plain-sum at widths 32-256 (72 runs)
Demos per task proportional to pi_k, minimum 10 (21 runs)
Random-label task added (21 runs)
LIBERO-90 frozen-ResNet-18 features, transformer heads d_model 32-512, uniform vs beta=1, scarcity, interventions (51 runs)
K-FAC low-curvature, high-curvature and random-direction edits at keep-mass 0.95, 0.9, 0.8, 0.6
Optional end-to-end LIBERO bc_transformer_policy, default and 4x smaller hidden size, x {uniform, beta=1}, 2 seeds (8 runs)

baseline.what: Same tasks under uniform sampling (beta=0) plus tuned plain-sum training and temperature upsampling at equal width

anchor.what: Reproduce the Huang et al. toy linear model: retained encoder features must match the analytic top-N utility set (Theorem 3) at every width [huang_html].
anchor.tolerance: At least 95% of features agree at every width; gradient norms respect the Theorem 4 bound

checks: Stage 0 toy must match theory before GPU spend (gate G0)
Metric unit tests: identical tasks cosine about 1, disjoint blocks about 0, M2 matches first-order -eta*g_rare*g_common within 5%
K-FAC subspace compared with exact Gauss-Newton eigendecomposition at width 32
G1: expert success at least 95% on fresh positions; width-2048 uniform policy at least 80% mean success
G2: width-512 uniform head at least 30% mean success with at least 30 of 90 tasks at 50% or more
G3: random-label task must lose performance before any real task under low-curvature removal
Ablating units assigned to task k must drop rollout success more than ablating random units (10 tasks per width)
Group projection must lower M1/M2 interference and raise rare-task success
Hypotheses H1-H5 and analysis script committed before the full sweeps

predictions.if_lever: Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.
predictions.if_not: Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.
predictions.decision_rule: M* = smallest M whose area skill score is within one standard error of the score at the largest M. W11 holds if M* <= 256 in every EnKF arm (E1, E2) and the skill lost to model error or gained from deep data exceeds the gain from M=32 to the largest M. Contradicted if in E2 or E4 the score still rises beyond M=1,024 by more than the E3 deep-data gain.
predictions.noise_rule: Area skill score averaged over 5 independent truths, with standard error across truths; M* defined within one standard error.
predictions.expected_why: The file expects skill to level off at tens to hundreds of members, with only the particle-filter arm plausibly continuing to gain.

plan.compute_tested_why: Ensemble size M, which parallel GPUs buy, is varied from 16 to 16,384 members, about 100 times beyond the published studies.
plan.scored_against: Molchan diagram area skill score of forecasts of full-rupture events in the hidden synthetic truth, compared with Poisson, periodic-recurrence, pattern-repeat, open-loop and oracle baselines.

plan.question: Do pretrained seismic models hold lab fault stress, friction and time to failure beyond what raw signal power gives, and does this grow with model size?
plan.hypothesis: Pretrained seismic models will hold fault-state information beyond signal power that grows with model size, though signal power alone already gives lab stress R² 0.82 [rouet2018].

compute_axis.quantity: Transformer parameters of the SeisLM-architecture model pretrained in-domain on lab acoustics at fixed data (Arm C sizes XS, S, M, L)

held_fixed: Pretraining tokens D about 3.2e10 for every size, 2 seeds per size
Pretraining corpus p4678 acoustic data; probe test on held-out p4679
Probe types (ridge and one-hidden-layer MLP), blocked cycle splits, window and layer chosen on validation cycles only
Decision rules written before test cycles are opened

predictions.if_lever: R² left after removing signal power rises steadily from smallest to largest model in both seeds, with smallest and largest confidence intervals not overlapping.
predictions.if_not: The size curve is flat, or pretrained probes sit within the confidence interval of random-init copies or the power baseline [rouet2018].
predictions.decision_rule: Lab-state-beyond-power requires pretrained minus random-init ΔR² >= 0.05 on held-out p4679 and p4678 transfer; scaling requires monotone residual R² rise XS to L in both seeds with L and XS CIs not overlapping.
predictions.noise_rule: 95% CIs by block bootstrap over stick-slip cycles; compare sizes only when seed-to-seed spread is smaller than the gap between sizes.
predictions.expected_why: The file does not state an expected outcome; it frames a null (nothing beyond a power meter) as a useful result too.

plan.compute_tested_why: Arm C varies model size at fixed small lab data (4 sizes, 2 seeds), but not data scale or SeisLM-scale training, which would cost $955 to $2,143.
plan.scored_against: Held-out stick-slip cycles (p4679, with p4678 transfer) scored against random-init twins and signal-power, scale-free-statistics and drift-only baselines; Arm B against event-metadata-only and a retrained ConvNet.

arms.what: Frozen SeisLM-base and SeisLM-large, linear and MLP probes vs randomly initialised copies, on Penn State lab experiments (p4679, p4678, p2394).
Same frozen models probed on Norcia 2016 foreshock/aftershock data (nine time classes at station NRCA) vs metadata-only baseline; lab-direction projection test.
SeisLM architecture pretrained from scratch at four sizes on p4678 acoustics, 2 seeds, then Arm A probes on p4679.

baseline.what: Log-variance (signal power) alone predicting shear stress on lab data

anchor.what: Random forest on window statistics reproduces time-to-failure R² about 0.89 on experiment p2394 (periodicity-only about 0.3) [rouet2017]
anchor.tolerance: Land near 0.89 (and near 0.3 for the periodicity model); a large miss means labels, sync or windows are wrong, so stop and fix before Arm C. No numeric tolerance given in the file.

checks: Reproduce published baselines on p2394 (B0, B2) and p4679 (B1, B2) before spending on Arm C
Acoustic/mechanical clock sync via acTime.txt; cross-correlate envelope with |dτ/dt|
Model loading: pinned-revision quickstart and regression tests; bf16 vs fp32 features cosine > 0.99 on 1,000 windows
Subsampling check on 200 cycles: encoding every 8th acquisition vs all, probe R² moves < 0.01
Planted-signal positive control, and about zero when plant absent
Blocked splits by whole cycles with purge gap of at least one window
Selectivity via circularly shifted labels; beyond-power residual test; amplitude-leak diagnostic (probe log-power)
Run-to-run transfer p4679 to p4678 with no refitting
LEACE erasure of stress subspace vs random subspace of same rank on a small TTF head
Arm B splits by event with time-blocked folds; metadata-only baseline B7
Check one p4678 file for same int8 layout as p4679 before Arm C

records.card: **O6 · Probe models for a latent fault state (Othello-style).** R3 · interp · top pick · compute tested: partly · plan expects: unsure · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Do pretrained seismic models hold lab fault stress, friction and time to failure beyond what raw signal power gives, and does this grow with model size? **What is known.** Rouet-Leduc et al. read lab fault state from window statistics with a random forest (time-to-failure R² 0.89, stress >0.9) [rouet2017]; Li et al. probed Othello networks against randomised ones [li2022]. No probing of seismic foundation models found. Whether pretrained seismic models represent fault state beyond signal power, and whether this grows with model size at fixed lab data. Coverage is limited since no web search was available. **Hypothesis.** Pretrained seismic models will hold fault-state information beyond signal power that grows with model size, though signal power alone already gives lab stress R² 0.82 [rouet2018]. **If compute is the lever.** R² left after removing signal power rises steadily from smallest to largest model in both seeds, with smallest and largest confidence intervals not overlapping. **If not.** The size curve is flat, or pretrained probes sit within the confidence interval of random-init copies or the power baseline [rouet2018]. **Test.** Probe frozen SeisLM models and random-init copies on Penn State lab stick-slip data for stress, friction and time to failure, beyond a power baseline. Check Norcia field data, and pretrain four model sizes in-domain to see if the signal grows. *Compute axis.* Transformer parameters of the SeisLM-architecture model pretrained in-domain on lab acoustics at fixed data (Arm C sizes XS, S, M, L): 0.8–85 million parameters, 4 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Random forest on window statistics reproduces time-to-failure R² about 0.89 on experiment p2394 (periodicity-only about 0.3) [rouet2017] Tolerance: Land near 0.89 (and near 0.3 for the periodicity model); a large miss means labels, sync or windows are wrong, so stop and fix before Arm C. [IF_LEVER, PLAN predictions] Residual R² after removing signal power must rise steadily with size in both seeds.
[IF_NOT, PLAN predictions] A flat size curve, or probes within random-init or power-baseline intervals, counts as a null.

plan.option_title: Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template)
plan.question: Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons?
plan.hypothesis: Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely.

compute_axis.quantity: SAE dictionary width (latents per SAE); the spike-in prevalence sweep is not a compute quantity

held_fixed: SeisLM-large released weights (12 layers, width 768, 90.7M params)
Layers 4, 8 and 12
BatchTopK mean k = 32
200M tokens per main-sweep SAE
30-s windows at 100 Hz, ZNE order, per-window normalisation
Score threshold fixed on validation split, reported on test split

predictions.if_lever: Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.if_not: The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.decision_rule: Stop after Stage 2 if pretrained SAE is about equal to B2 or B0/B1 match the SAE on inspection cost for most known classes; stop after Stage 3 if no class reaches best-latent F1 >= 0.5 at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.noise_rule: 3 seeds per main SAE (2 for spike-in); a candidate latent must appear in at least 2 of 3 seeds; threshold frozen on period A and replicated on period B; blind review by two seismologists at 80% accuracy.
predictions.expected_why: The file expects known classes and missed instances of them to be recovered but a genuinely new class to be unlikely, and gives no expected outcome for the baseline comparison.

plan.compute_tested_why: The plan varies SAE width (16,384 vs 65,536) but its key test varies class prevalence (0%, 0.1%, 1%, 10%) in the training mix, which more parallel compute does not buy.
plan.scored_against: Held-out labels (F1 and AUROC), injected synthetic artifacts, spike-in recovery, hidden-event lists (445 PNW noise traces, Suarez and Beroza error list), baselines B0-B4, and SeisLM's own spliced contrastive loss versus matched-rank PCA.

arms.what: BatchTopK SAEs (plus ReLU/L1) on SeisLM-large layers 4, 8, 12
Log-spectrogram or scattering features, PCA and Gaussian-mixture clustering (B0'; band-limited energy for tremor)
Single neurons, PCA components, k-means on the same activations
Same SAE recipe on a randomly initialised SeisLM
Supervised logistic probe per label on raw activations (ceiling)
PhaseNet + EQTransformer ensemble, hidden-event test only

baseline.what: Spectrogram/scattering clustering (B0) and single-neuron/PCA/k-means (B1) inspection cost on known classes

anchor.what: SeisLM repo regression check reports exact equality between portable bundles and original checkpoints; paper's noise-vs-earthquake separation (pretrained vs random-init) reproduces on STEAD.
anchor.tolerance: exact equality for the regression check; separation qualitatively reproduces

checks: Fraction of variance explained, mean L0 and dead-latent fraction for every SAE
Spliced-loss test: replace layer output with SAE reconstruction, recompute SeisLM masked contrastive loss, compare to clean loss and to matched-rank PCA reconstruction
Synthetic artifacts (spikes, DC steps, clipping, calibration signals, zeroed segments) injected into clean noise; a dedicated latent must respond and rise with amplitude
0% prevalence spike-in arm as floor

Seven gates for a candidate new class: seed stability, not a known label (best F1 < 0.3), not metadata (AUROC < 0.7), multi-station coherence (3 or more stations), not SAE geometry artifact, blind review (>= 80%), replication in period B

phases.what: Stage 0: literature check (one hour), environment, regression and smoke tests, throughput benchmark

gate.else: Stop if the regression check fails or the noise/earthquake separation does not reproduce (spend about $34).

phases.what: Stage 1: download about 300 GB (SeisBench subset plus continuous data), window and normalise, cache activations for 3 layers
Stage 2: 24 SAEs (sweep, ReLU, random-init); baselines B0-B3; alignment tables; inspection-cost comparison
phases.stop_rule: Stop (about $317 spent) if pretrained SAE is about equal to B2, or B0/B1 match the SAE on inspection cost for most known classes.

phases.what: Stage 3: spike-in detection limit, 3 classes x 4 prevalences x 2 seeds
phases.stop_rule: Stop (about $369 spent) if no class gets a dedicated latent (F1 >= 0.5) at 1% prevalence or below.

phases.what: Stage 4: encode continuous data; gates 1-5 and 7; evidence packets. Gate 6 blind review is done by analysts after the instance is terminated.

records.card: **O7 · Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template).** R3 · interp · random pick · compute tested: partly · plan expects: unsure · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons? **What is known.** Goodfire's Evo 2 SAE work and InterPLM on protein models; no seismic SAE result was found, but no web search was run, so one may exist. Whether SAEs on a seismic foundation model give latents that beat spectrogram clustering, and how rare a class can be and still get its own latent. **Hypothesis.** Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely. **If compute is the lever.** Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below. **If not.** The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below. **Test.** Train sparse autoencoders on three layers of SeisLM-large, score features against known labels, measure how rare a class can be and still get a feature, then scan Cascadia and Parkfield data, all on one H100 for about $700. *Compute axis.* SAE dictionary width (latents per SAE); the spike-in prevalence sweep is not a compute quantity: 16,384–65,536 latents, 2 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** SeisLM repo regression check reports exact equality between portable bundles and original checkpoints; paper's noise-vs-earthquake separation (pretrained vs random-init) reproduces on STEAD. Tolerance: exact equality for the regression check; separation qualitatively reproduces. **Would not show.** No web search was run, so earlier seismic SAE work cannot be ruled out. Data-size and token-count figures are the file's inferences, not measured. predictions.if_lever: More compute buys more independent residue checks of D(9); at most about 5 primes fit, and 19 primes would rebuild D(9) exactly by Chinese remainder theorem.

The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one? **Producer file.** [producer.md](/home/hal/stage/runs-v3/seed-1/R4/physical/c70bfb85/producer.md)

fields.question: Can D(9), the ninth Dedekind number, be recomputed modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores for far less than the published FP64 cost, within $1,000?
fields.hypothesis: Switching Jäkel's matrix formula from FP64 to exact INT8/INT32 modular arithmetic cuts the cost per check enough that a few residues of D(9) fit in $1,000.
fields.restructuring.method: Interval classes and prime residues are independent sums, so 9,919 classes share one queue across 8 GPUs, and the matrices are built once and reused for every prime.
fields.predictions.if_lever: More compute buys more independent residue checks of D(9); at most about 5 primes fit, and 19 primes would rebuild D(9) exactly by Chinese remainder theorem.
fields.predictions.if_not: One residue costs more than $750 (memory traffic and O(m²) work keep efficiency low), so the budget buys no full residue, only the measured cost curve.
fields.test_summary: Reimplement Jäkel's D(9) formula modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores, benchmark against his FP64 path on one GPU, then spend up to $750 on 8 GPUs computing residues and compare each with the published value.
fields.novelty.closest_prior: Jäkel computed D(9) with FP64 batched DGEMM on A100s in 5,311 GPU-hours [jakel]; Ootomo et al. emulate DGEMM on integer tensor cores [ootomo].
fields.anchor.what: Published D(9) value reduces to 6 mod 210, matching the proven congruences mod 2, 3, 5 and 7 [pawelski]; small-n d(4)..d(8) must also be reproduced.
fields.limits: Result measures cost and agreement mod a few primes, not a full independent D(9). Cost estimates assume Jäkel's efficiency and hardware spec readings that are uncertain. Web search was unavailable, so post-2023 work may be missed.

fields.limits: One model on one node; a flat curve may reflect this test setup, not missing library coverage. With 100 problems per set, gains of 2-3 problems are noise. Absolute scores may be inflated by training-data contamination.

pick.title: Latent-knowledge probes for statement fidelity

plan.option_title: O3: does the model know its Lean differs from the English?
plan.question: Can a linear probe on a model's activations detect misformalized Lean statements better than the model's own Yes/No answer, a Lean-only probe, or a strong LLM judge?
plan.hypothesis: A probe on a 32B model's activations separates wrong from fixed Lean better than the model's own verdict, because models may know more than they say [mallen].

compute_axis.quantity: Rented 4x B200 instance-hours (the plan's total GPU time); the experiment does not vary it

held_fixed: Same Formal Conjectures train/test split grouped by PR and problem file
Same auditor prompt and Lean-only and mismatched-informal control prompts
Pre-fixed decision thresholds (set before looking at test data)
Temporal test sets starting after each model's release

predictions.if_lever: Probe AUROC reaches at least 0.75 on fixes made after model release, beats the model's own verdict by 0.05, and catches 25% of the strong judge's misses.
predictions.if_not: Probe gains vanish when the informal statement is removed (gap at most 0.03), or probe and judge miss the same items, as the skeptic's concern says.
predictions.decision_rule: O3 is a real second channel if transfer-probe AUROC >= 0.75 on post-cutoff fixes, Delta-control >= 0.10, probe beats B1 by >= 0.05, and it catches >= 25% of B4's misses with McNemar p < 0.05. O3 reads style, not fidelity, if Delta-control <= 0.03 or B0 ~ probe.
predictions.noise_rule: Bootstrap CIs resampling PRs; Hanley-McNeil half-width about +/-0.04 at 300 pairs; probe fitting rerun with three seeds and fold assignments; judges sampled k=4; margins of 0.05-0.10 set above the CI half-width.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it says only that GPUs are not the binding input and that labels and Lean-literate review are.

plan.compute_tested_why: The plan tests whether a probe beats other detectors, not how results change with more compute. The file says GPUs are not the binding input (NOT-COMPUTE-BOUND verdict).
plan.scored_against: Human-fixed labels: Formal Conjectures merged misformalization PRs (wrong Lean before, fixed Lean after), plus CriticLeanBench labels and a few PutnamBench fixes.

arms.what: Difference-of-means and logistic-regression probes on residual activations of Qwen3-32B, Goedel-Formalizer-V2-32B and CriticLeanGPT-Qwen3-32B-RL
Character n-gram logistic regression plus length features on the Lean text alone
Each model's own verbalized P(No), zero-shot and k-shot
Goedel-Formalizer length-normalized log-likelihood of the Lean
CriticLeanGPT-Qwen3-32B-RL with reasoning, k=4
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 with reasoning, k=4
Optional: Leanstral 1.5 via its free API endpoint, no activations
Stretch: probe on Leanstral-1.5-119B-A6B via vLLM apply_model hooks

baseline.what: Strong LLM judge DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 with reasoning (B4), plus the model's own Yes/No verdict (B1)

anchor.what: Reproduce a Geometry of Truth result on Qwen3-32B: difference-of-means probes separate true from false statements and transfer across datasets [gotruth].
anchor.tolerance: No numeric tolerance stated in the file; if it fails the pipeline is buggy, not O3.

checks: Geometry of Truth pipeline sanity check on Qwen3-32B
Batched vs unbatched activations match to fp16 tolerance on 20 items
Positive control: FormalAlign random pairing should be near-trivial for probe and judges
Shuffled labels give AUROC about 0.5
Hewitt-Liang control task, report selectivity
Lean-only, mismatched-informal and B0 confound controls
Leakage: group splits by PR, file and author; temporal test sets; compare pre- and post-release fixes
Label audit of 50 random triples (agreement at least 90%) and 50 synthetic mutants for equivalence
Inspect the 20 highest-scoring fixed items and 20 lowest-scoring wrong items
Three seeds and fold assignments for probe fitting; judges k=4

fields.question: Can a linear probe on a model's activations detect misformalized Lean statements better than the model's own Yes/No answer, a Lean-only probe, or a strong LLM judge?
fields.hypothesis: A probe on a 32B model's activations separates wrong from fixed Lean better than the model's own verdict, because models may know more than they say [mallen].
fields.predictions.if_lever: Probe AUROC reaches at least 0.75 on fixes made after model release, beats the model's own verdict by 0.05, and catches 25% of the strong judge's misses.
fields.predictions.if_not: Probe gains vanish when the informal statement is removed (gap at most 0.03), or probe and judge miss the same items, as the skeptic's concern says.
fields.novelty.closest_prior: Mallen et al. found probes usually report a model's knowledge independently of its output; Goodfire used difference-of-means from synthetic code to detect real reward hacking [mallen]. Neither tested Lean statement fidelity.
fields.limits: Fixed statements may differ from wrong ones in style, not fidelity. One author wrote 268 of 515 PRs and 239 were merged in one month. A fixed statement may still be wrong, inflating false-positive rates.

plan.question: Do a model's hidden states for an English statement and its Lean formalization drift apart when the formalization is wrong, and is that more useful than a text judge or cheap baselines?
plan.hypothesis: Expected to fail on fine-grained errors: English-Lean hidden-state similarity likely reflects only topic, as similarity alone did far worse than likelihood alone in [formalalign].

held_fixed: Input normalization: attributes, comments and proofs stripped, theorem name replaced with X, identical formatting for W and F, no chat template
Layer, pooling and normalization chosen by 5-fold CV grouped by PR before any test fold is scored
Cap of 3 pairs per PR, bootstrap clustered by PR
Decision rule fixed before the run

predictions.if_lever: Hidden-state similarity beats the best word-overlap, embedding and likelihood baselines by at least 10 points on fixed-versus-wrong pairs and catches at least 25% of errors the judge missed.
predictions.if_not: Similarity separates matched from random pairs only (topic level), fails to beat cheap baselines on fine pairs, and is redundant with the text judge.
predictions.decision_rule: C1 gate: matched-vs-random AUROC >= 0.90 at best layer for at least one model, else stop. C2 passes if best O4 variant beats best of B1, B2, B3 by >= 10 points two-alternative accuracy (95% cluster-bootstrap CI excluding 0), English-ablated control within 50 +/- 5%, and invariance ratio <= 0.5. C3 passes if O4 flags >= 25% of judge-accepted incorrect items at the judge's false-positive rate and judge+O4 raises AUROC by >= 0.02 with CI excluding 0 on both external sets.
predictions.noise_rule: 95% bootstrap intervals clustered by PR (FC) or problem ID (ProofNetVerif); paired differences use the same bootstrap; Holm correction across the three core models.
predictions.expected_why: FormalAlign found the representation-similarity term alone far worse than the likelihood term, and interp.md doubts fine-grained separation.

plan.compute_tested_why: The test compares scoring methods (activations vs text judge vs baselines) across models and layers; it does not vary a quantity that more parallel compute buys.
plan.scored_against: Human-triaged Formal Conjectures fix pairs (wrong vs fixed Lean), ProofNetVerif and CriticLeanBench labels, and the Qwen3-32B text judge, plus lexical, embedding, likelihood baselines and a supervised probe ceiling.

fields.question: Do a model's hidden states for an English statement and its Lean formalization drift apart when the formalization is wrong, and is that more useful than a text judge or cheap baselines?
fields.hypothesis: Expected to fail on fine-grained errors: English-Lean hidden-state similarity likely reflects only topic, as similarity alone did far worse than likelihood alone in [formalalign].
fields.predictions.if_lever: Hidden-state similarity beats the best word-overlap, embedding and likelihood baselines by at least 10 points on fixed-versus-wrong pairs and catches at least 25% of errors the judge missed.
fields.test_summary: Compare English and Lean hidden states in Qwen3-32B, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B and Kimina-7B on 715 mined wrong-to-fixed pairs and two benchmarks, against the same model as text judge and cheap baselines [formalalign].
fields.limits: Positives are only errors already found, biased toward what judges find. Small named slices (density, Euclidean) are checked item by item only. Results show detecting errors the model's own reading exposes, not misformalization in general.

plan.option_title: Turbulent fluid flow (direct numerical simulation)
plan.question: On one rented GPU node, does the cost of direct simulation grow as Reynolds number to the sixth power, and does finer resolution remove the error a turbulence model leaves?
plan.hypothesis: Compute buys fidelity for small-scale statistics that closures discard, while cheap closures stay cheaper for large-scale quantities at modest Reynolds number.

compute_axis.quantity: Grid points per side N: at fixed viscosity (Q2) and with Reynolds number rising at fixed k_max*eta (Q1)

held_fixed: JHTDB 1024^3 viscosity 0.000185 in the fixed-physics ladder (Q2)
Forcing: hold total energy in modes |k|<=2 constant
Time scheme: integrating factor plus second-order Adams-Bashforth
Dealiasing: phase shift plus 2*sqrt(2)/3 truncation
k_max*eta about 1.35 in the Reynolds ladder (Q1)

predictions.if_lever: Fully resolved simulation matches the published 1024^3 statistics within tolerance. Unmodeled simulation error in velocity-gradient statistics falls as grid size N grows, while large-eddy simulation keeps an error floor.
predictions.if_not: Smagorinsky LES matches gradient statistics at equal cost, or resolved DNS misses the published statistics, so extra resolution does not remove closure error.
predictions.decision_rule: Reproduction passes if Re_lambda is within 4% of 418, E_tot within 3% of 0.705 and epsilon within 10% of 0.103. Lever holds if no-model DNS error in gradient skewness and flatness falls with N while LES at every tested constant keeps an error floor.
predictions.noise_rule: Pass limits come from variability in the published time series (Re_lambda SD 10.8; epsilon moves about 10% between 1 T_L and 5 T_L averaging). Average over at least 10 T_L; widen spectrum tolerance to 3x own block-to-block standard error if larger.
predictions.expected_why: The file predicts compute buys fidelity for gradient quantities the closure throws away, while LES stays cheaper for large-scale quantities.

plan.compute_tested_why: Grid size N, which more GPUs and memory buy, is raised from 128 to 1024 (2048 gated), and cost per turnover is measured against it.
plan.scored_against: JHTDB 1024^3 published statistics (README values, spectrum.txt, time series), plus Taylor-Green Re=1600 reference dissipation and exact-solution tests.

Tier 2: Taylor-Green Re=1600 peak dissipation within 2.5% at 256^3 and 1% at 512^3

fields.limits: Reaches Taylor-scale Reynolds number about 420, perhaps 660 briefly; cannot move the research frontier. Cost figures are model estimates until the benchmark phase measures them. The reference describes the forcing in one sentence, so box size and large-eddy turnover time may differ by a few percent.

pick.title: Learned weather emulators (GraphCast)

plan.option_title: Medium-range weather forecasting with learned models
plan.question: At 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget, does GraphCast-style forecast skill improve more from 4 times the training compute or from 4 times the years of reanalysis data?
plan.hypothesis: Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794].

compute_axis.quantity: training compute per run as a fraction of T (about 21 GPU-hours on one H100), at 40 years of data

held_fixed: Architecture: GraphCast_small processor (config A, latent 512) or config B (latent 256) chosen once by pilot throughput
Optimizer: AdamW, betas 0.9/0.95, weight decay 0.1, clip 32, 1,000-step warmup to 1e-3, half-cosine decay
Normalization statistics: DeepMind's published files, same for every run
Splits: validation 2019, test 2020, scored once
Evaluation: WB2 evaluate.py on 732 forecasts in 2020
Last 10% of each run's wall-clock on 2 to 4 rollout steps
Loss: GraphCast level-weighted MSE

predictions.if_lever: The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise.
predictions.if_not: D exceeds C by more than twice the seed noise (data-bound), or neither exceeds the other by that margin (inconclusive).
predictions.decision_rule: C = RMSE(40y, T/4) - RMSE(40y, T); D = RMSE(10y recent, T) - RMSE(40y, T). C > D + 2N: compute-bound. D > C + 2N: data-bound. Otherwise inconclusive.
predictions.noise_rule: N = |seed 0 - seed 1| per metric and lead time from the two 40-year runs. Effects smaller than 2N are reported as null. Paired per-forecast differences with a one-week block bootstrap.
predictions.expected_why: The file predicts that 4x compute at 40 years beats 4x data, since GraphCast's authors found older data of little benefit.

plan.compute_tested_why: Runs at T/4, T/2 and T on the same 40-year data directly vary training compute, which more parallel GPUs buy.
plan.scored_against: Day 1/3/5/10 RMSE and ACC on 2020 against ERA5 (WB2 convention), compared with WB2 published baselines and with the in-experiment 40-year full-compute run (two seeds).

A matched comparison of years of reanalysis versus training compute, same architecture and evaluation, at 1.5 degrees. The file found none, but its web search was exhausted. **Hypothesis.** Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794]. **If compute is the lever.** The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise. **If not.** D exceeds C by more than twice the seed noise (data-bound), or neither exceeds the other by that margin (inconclusive). **Test.** Train ten GraphCast-style models at 1.5 degrees on one 8x H100 machine, varying years of ERA5 data (5 to 40) and compute (1/4 to 1x). Compare day-5 Z500 error gains from compute and data against seed noise and WB2 baselines. *Compute axis.* Training compute per run as a fraction of T (about 21 GPU-hours on one H100), at 40 years of data: 0.25–1 fraction of T, 3 levels. records.writer_text:
[QUESTION, GIVEN root question] The root question asks what limits robot manipulation, and whether raw compute can close the gap.
[QUESTION, PLAN question] This test uses weather forecasting as a stand-in, at 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget.
[QUESTION, PLAN question] Does forecast skill improve more from quadrupling training compute or from quadrupling the years of reanalysis data?
[HYPOTHESIS, PLAN hypothesis] Quadrupling compute at 40 years should improve day-5 height error more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years.
[HYPOTHESIS, SOURCE graphcast] The reasoning is that the 40-year record is near saturation, since older data helped GraphCast little.
[TEST, PLAN arms] Eight GPUs on one machine train models on 5 to 40 years of data.
[TEST, PLAN compute_axis] Compute runs at a quarter, a half, and the full level, a span of 4.
[TEST, PLAN arms] Two full runs with different seeds set the noise floor.
[TEST, PLAN numbers] Planned spend is $834.46 over 39 machine-hours, leaving $165.54 unallocated as contingency.
[TEST, PLAN anchor] Our scoring code must first reproduce published 2020 benchmark scores within half a percent.
[IF_LEVER, PLAN predictions] Compute is the lever if its gain beats the data gain by more than twice the seed noise.
[IF_NOT, PLAN predictions] If the data gain wins by that margin, forecasting is data-bound.
[IF_NOT, PLAN predictions] If neither wins by that margin, the result is inconclusive.
[LIMITS, PLAN scope_gap] Reproducing full GraphCast training would cost $69,000, about 69 times this budget.
[LIMITS, PLAN limits] Only one resolution, one architecture family, and two seeds are tested.
[LIMITS, PLAN scope_gap] The test says nothing direct about robotics; the link is only an analogy.
[LIMITS, PLAN novelty] A matched prior comparison may exist that the search did not find.

fields.question: At 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget, does GraphCast-style forecast skill improve more from 4 times the training compute or from 4 times the years of reanalysis data?
fields.hypothesis: Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794].
fields.predictions.if_lever: The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise.
fields.test_summary: Train ten GraphCast-style models at 1.5 degrees on one 8x H100 machine, varying years of ERA5 data (5 to 40) and compute (1/4 to 1x). Compare day-5 Z500 error gains from compute and data against seed noise and WB2 baselines.
fields.novelty.closest_prior: GraphCast's authors found adding 1959-1978 data had little benefit, and ArchesWeather found older ERA5 harder to fit; neither varied years of data against compute under one setup [arXiv 2212.12794, 2405.14527].
fields.anchor.what: Our evaluation code run on WB2's stored 2020 forecasts reproduces published scores: GraphCast T2M day 5 = 1.252, HRES T2M = 1.334, HRES Z500 = 304.35.
fields.limits: Single resolution (1.5 degrees) and one architecture family. Fixed small budget; day-10 RMSE differences may reflect blur, not skill. Only two seeds, at one configuration; a 2025-2026 reproduction may exist unfound.

pick.title: Symbolic distillation of learned simulators to fix the model class M

plan.option_title: I3 made concrete: symbolic distillation of a learned simulator to fix the model class M, on at most $1,000 of Lambda GPU time
plan.question: Can equations distilled from a learned correction to an analytic pushing model generalize as well as the neural correction, and recover known friction physics?
plan.hypothesis: A sparse neural friction correction, replaced by closed-form equations, should generalize at least as well as the network, matching [cranmer]'s dark-matter result.

compute_axis.quantity: PySR search budget in Phase 1 (36 runs of about 30 core-hours each); more GPUs only shorten wall-clock

held_fixed: Inputs to the correction function, operator set (+, -, x, /, square, sqrt, exp, log, abs, tanh), maximum expression size 25 and equation selection rule, all frozen before any real-data PySR run
Evaluation metrics: translation error percent, position error mm, rotation error degrees, open-loop
Splits chosen in advance: in-distribution, speed OOD, acceleration OOD, shape OOD
5000 samples per material and split for PySR; 3 search seeds, term accepted only if in at least 2 of 3

predictions.if_lever: Not a compute-lever test; more compute would only shorten wall-clock, not change the equations found.
predictions.if_not: Equations recover the known friction signatures and beat the analytic model out of distribution, matching the neural hybrid [ajay]; gains come from structure, not GPUs.
predictions.decision_rule: Gate 4 passes if the symbolic model beats the analytic model B0 on every split, is no worse than hybrid B3 on the speed and shape splits, and a shared form refit per material stays within 10% of per-material error on at least 3 of 4 materials. Gate 1 needs recovery of injected terms with constants within 10% in at least 4 of 5 seeds.
predictions.noise_rule: 5 training seeds and 3 PySR seeds; terms must appear in at least 2 of 3 PySR seeds; shuffled-material control; errors reported relative to the 3.4-11.7 mm repeat-push spread.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it lists outcome readings for each gate result.

plan.compute_tested_why: The file says eight GPUs buy wall-clock time, not results: workload is small networks plus CPU-bound symbolic regression, so the test varies model structure, not parallel compute.
plan.scored_against: Neural-residual hybrid B3 and analytic B0 on the same splits, plus independent friction measurements (speed dependence, anisotropy) from the push-dataset paper and the force-torque sensor.

arms.what: Analytic quasi-static pusher-slider with ellipsoidal limit surface; friction parameters fitted per material by least squares
Optional: B0 with a convex polynomial limit surface identified from data
Black-box recurrent network (Ajay et al.'s Neural)
B0 plus neural residual (Ajay et al.'s Hybrid, deterministic); main baseline
PySR or SINDy run directly on B0's per-step residual accelerations, no network
B0 plus an L1-gated, L1-penalized MLP correction to the support friction wrench, trained on kinematics only
S with the correction replaced by the PySR expression chosen by Cranmer's selection rule, constants refit then frozen; the deliverable

baseline.what: Hybrid (analytic + neural residual) on rect1 on ABS test set, position error in mm (rotation 2.03 deg)

anchor.what: Reproduce the analytic model's position error on rect1 on ABS from [ajay]; neural 2.81 mm and hybrid 2.04 mm also checked.
anchor.tolerance: within about 25%

checks: Gate 0: B0, B2, B3 within about 25% of 6.91 / 2.81 / 2.04 mm on rect1 on ABS

Gate 1: synthetic injected friction terms (speed-dependent, world-frame anisotropy, spatial map) recovered with constants within 10% in at least 4 of 5 seeds; null control returns no term in at least 4 of 5 seeds; one two-term confounding case
Gate 2: latent contact force vs force sensor R^2 >= 0.9 on held-out quasi-static pushes
Gate 3: positive speed term for pu and none for ABS/Delrin; cos 2phi term for pu with max/min ratio between 1.3 and 1.7 and below 10% anisotropy for ABS/Delrin, without the table as input
Gate 4: generalization splits and pass conditions as in decision rule
Shuffled-material control; accepted friction terms must dissipate energy (negative dissipation deviation on ABS is a red flag); drop unreliable-list files

Gate 5 (cloth, only if friction passes): distilled edge term added to PhysTwin simulator, evaluated against 0.012 / 0.022 / 72.5 and 0.013 / 0.018, then against 0.061 (SOFA linen) and 0.067 (MuJoCo chequered) on the fling

phases.what: Development, measure actual time per run, reproduce baselines (Gate 0), synthetic positive and negative controls (Gate 1); rescale estimates before renting any 8-GPU machine.
phases.stop_rule: If Gate 0 or Gate 1 fails, stop; I3 is not testable on this data.

phases.what: Friction on the MIT push dataset: train B2, B3, S over 4 materials x 3 split families x 5 seeds; PySR 36 runs; Gates 2, 3, 4.
phases.stop_rule: Proceed to Phase 2 only if Phase 1 gates pass; spend hard stop at $1,000.

phases.what: Cloth (only if Phase 1 passes): graph network on PhysTwin spring graph with L1-penalized residual and lagged strain; 30 GNN runs, 10 PySR runs; Gate 5.

plan.question: Can a cheap activation probe on a diffusion policy rank robot demonstrations as well as gradient-based CUPID influence, at far lower scoring cost?
plan.hypothesis: A difference-of-means probe on policy activations (ActProbe) may match gradient influence at about a tenth of the cost, as in language models [goodfire_probe].

held_fixed: Square MH low-dim, 192 training demos in the filtering base
100 scoring rollouts per base policy
500 evaluation rollouts per retrained policy on a disjoint seed range from 1,000,000
CUPID tuned epoch counts per ratio: 2,001, 2,551, 3,051
Hook point, diffusion step k=10, J=4 noise draws fixed in advance

predictions.if_lever: ActProbe within 3 points of CUPID, at least 5 above Random; StateProbe, Demo-SCORE at least 3 lower; cost at most 1/10 TRAK's.
predictions.if_not: ActProbe about equals Demo-SCORE and StateProbe (gain comes from rollout labels), or about equals Random while CUPID beats Random (gradients carry more information).
predictions.decision_rule: At Square 50% filtered: ActProbe >= CUPID - 3 points, ActProbe >= Random + 5 points, StateProbe and Demo-SCORE >= 3 points below ActProbe, and ActProbe scoring cost <= 1/10 of TRAK.
predictions.noise_rule: Paired by seed over 3 seeds x 500 rollouts, every seed reported; binomial SE about 1.8 points at 80% success; a 3-point gap is only suggestive; spare budget buys 2 extra seeds. Shuffled-label control must land within 3 points of Random.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it notes ActProbe is close to Demo-SCORE and may look weakest at 25% filtering.

plan.compute_tested_why: The plan varies the filtering ratio and compares scoring cost (activation vs gradient), not parallel compute; the cost ratio is measured by logging GPU-seconds per method.

**W11 · Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case).** R3 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever

**Question.** On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?

**What is known.** van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model. Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter.

**Hypothesis.** Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

**Restructuring.** Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle. Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.

**If compute is the lever.** Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.

**If not.** Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

**Test.** Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].

*Compute axis.* Ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run): 16–16,384 members, 10 levels. Closest prior: 150 [van_dinther], beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

**Check first.** A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations. Tolerance: within 1% on recurrence interval and first-event time.

**Would not show.** A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

*Cost.* Plans $684.14 of the $1,000 budget over 26 machine-hours, leaving $315.86. Main guess: Wall time on 8x H100, main truth [g], measured after $25.74 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.9× higher. 2 cost flags in the block.

**W13 · Training robot foundation models and video world models.** R2 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken

**Question.** With data held fixed, does more fine-tuning compute raise task success of a small robot vision-language-action model in simulation, or does data limit it?

**What is known.** SmolVLA paper reports LIBERO results at 0.24B/0.45B/2.25B sizes and says it can train for far fewer steps without significant loss, but gives no step or data grid [smolvla_paper]. Whether, at fixed data, more fine-tuning steps help SmolVLA on LIBERO, and how steps trade against data fraction, capacity and a removed camera.

**Hypothesis.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844].

**If compute is the lever.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success.

**If not.** At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points.

**Test.** Fine-tune SmolVLA on LIBERO in 25 runs, varying steps (5k, 15k, 50k) and data (10 to 100%) independently, plus capacity, camera removal and pretraining arms. Score 27 checkpoints on 2,000 rollouts each against a published 87.3% baseline.

*Compute axis.* Training steps per run (with fixed cosine schedule per run), crossed with data fraction; also trainable parameters in arm C: 5,000–50,000 steps, 3 levels. Closest prior: 100,000 [smolvla_paper], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 1200 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%. Tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3.

**Would not show.** Small simulated benchmark, one model family; may not transfer to larger models or real robots. Training and evaluation speed unmeasured, so cost may rise. 87.3% replication may miss; schedule unpublished.

*Cost.* Plans $557.20 of the $1,000 budget over 35 machine-hours, leaving $442.80. Full scale: Cosmos world-model training on 10,000 H100 GPUs for three months; file says $1,000 is about 1/86,000 of it, $86M, 86,000× the budget. 5 cost flags in the block.

**I1 · Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer.** R1 · interp · top pick · compute tested: no · plan expects: unsure · halted: G-plan

**Question.** Do released entity-hallucination probes flag invented entities in an open model's paper reviews better than cheap baselines, especially where citation lookup cannot settle the case?

**What is known.** Obeso et al. trained entity-hallucination probes on LongFact-style long-form generation, with Llama-3.3-70B linear AUC 0.8667 and LoRA 0.9048; they did not test paper reviews [obeso]. Whether the probes transfer to long-context paper reviews and add value over lookups on entities that lookups cannot settle.

**Hypothesis.** Probes help only on entities that are hard to look up; the released 70B probe should reach AUC 0.80 on review entities and beat the best cheap baseline by 0.05 there.

**If the hypothesis holds.** Released 70B probe reaches AUC at least 0.80 on hard-to-look-up entities and beats the best cheap baseline by at least 0.05, with a confidence interval excluding 0.

**If not.** Probe falls below 0.80 or beats the best baseline by under 0.05; or retrieval leaves under 1% fabricated citations, so lookup suffices [AAAI-26].

**Test.** Generate about 2,800 reviews per model of 1,200 2025 ML papers with Llama-3.3-70B and 3.1-8B, label entities, then compare released and retrained probes with four cheap baselines, gated by replication, audits and controls.

*Compute axis.* Reviewer model size (Llama 8B vs 70B), the only axis the plan varies; the claim concerns probe quality, not compute: 8–70 billion parameters, 2 levels. Closest prior: 70 [obeso], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Released probes on Obeso's LongFact test split must reproduce reported AUC: 70B linear 0.8667, 70B LoRA 0.9048, 8B linear 0.8535, 8B LoRA 0.8938 [obeso]. Tolerance: within +/-0.02 AUC.

**Would not show.** Labels come from automatic lookups and an open-weight judge, audited on only 300 entities, so label noise caps measurable AUC. Retrieval-equipped reviewers rarely fabricate, so fabricated entities may be too few. Only Llama 8B and 70B reviewers on 2025 ML papers are tested.

*Cost.* Plans $440.23 of the $1,000 budget over 23 machine-hours, leaving $559.77. Full scale: Obeso-style labelling (Claude Sonnet 4 with web search) of all 5,600 reviews at about $0.70 each, $3,900, 3.9× the budget. 17 cost flags in the block.
